title: The long-run price of committing before seeing the future
shortTitle: Rent today, or commit for the season?
oneLine: An unrefereed candidate proves a limiting guarantee for i.i.d. prophet inequalities over time, with certified bounds below the inverse golden ratio.
abstract: An online decision maker rents one resource over a finite horizon, observing independent nonnegative offers from a known common distribution with finite positive mean. The optimal expected reward is compared with a prophet who knows every offer. This candidate proves that the worst-case ratio converges as the horizon grows, identifies the limit with a continuum minimax value, and shows that deterministic threshold schedules approach that value arbitrarily closely. Explicit Arb-certified witnesses give 0.60922 <= gamma* <= 0.609816, strictly below the inverse golden ratio. No exact constant or attainment by a bounded schedule is established. Atomic distributions may require randomised threshold-tie handling. A separate million-period instance gives ratio at most 0.6123450.

keyResults: The worst-case optimal-online-to-prophet ratio has a limit as the number of periods tends to infinity.
The limit equals a continuum profile infimum and a cumulative-coverage minimax value.
Deterministic threshold schedules approach the limit; attainment by one bounded schedule is not proved, and atomic laws may require randomised ties.
A separate finite witness at one million periods certifies a ratio at most 0.6123450; it is not the asymptotic upper bound.

narration: How much is hindsight worth when a decision lasts? An Evidence Press audio briefing. Imagine lending out one machine. Each day brings a new offer. You know the distribution of offers, but not tomorrow's price. You can rent the machine for one day and reconsider, or commit it for the rest of the season at today's daily rate. A prophet knows every future offer in advance. This mathematical model assumes independent offers from the same known distribution, with nonnegative values and a finite, positive average. It asks how much of the prophet's expected earnings an optimal online strategy can guarantee against the hardest distribution. The candidate proves that this worst-case ratio approaches a limit as the season grows longer. It characterises the limit through a continuous-time competition between threshold strategies and difficult value distributions. Explicit witnesses, checked with arithmetic that encloses rounding errors, place the limit between sixty point nine two two percent and sixty point nine eight one six percent. That is below the inverse golden ratio, roughly sixty-one point eight percent. The interval is certified, but the exact constant remains unknown. The proof also shows that deterministic threshold schedules can approach the limiting value as closely as desired. It does not produce one schedule proved to attain that value. Distributions with repeated values can still require randomisation when breaking threshold ties. These are long-horizon statements, not guarantees at every finite season length. A separate million-period example gives a different upper bound, and the general convergence estimate is too coarse for practical timing advice. This is AI-assisted, unrefereed mathematics. Written proofs and numerical certificates have different roles; neither establishes real-world rental performance. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.
